provenance.title: Adult bedside medical procedures — is this the right procedure for this patient, and what does the result mean
provenance.primarySource: EDLIZ / Zimbabwe standard treatment guidelines and standard procedural safety practice
provenance.why: A bedside procedure — a lumbar puncture, a diagnostic tap, a pleural aspiration — is only safe when it is the right procedure for this patient and the timing is right. Two questions decide that, and they are the ones a busy ward most often skips: is there a contraindication that must be cleared first (raised intracranial pressure before an LP, a bleeding risk before any needle), and once the sample is taken, what does it mean. This pack owns the indication and the interpretation; the procedures-service owns actually doing it. Keeping the appropriateness decision as reviewable data rather than tribal knowledge is the point — an LP into raised intracranial pressure can cone the brainstem, and a needle into a coagulopathic patient bleeds, so the order of operations is a safety property, not a preference.

sourceVerification.note: EDLIZ (2015) and the national procedural safety standards are NOT vendored under docs/reference/who-dak/MANIFEST.json — there is no WHO DAK for adult bedside procedural appropriateness, so these rules are national additions authored against EDLIZ and standard practice. The thresholds and contraindication lists here are engineering placeholders and ship ENGINEERING_SEED until the primary text is vendored and MOHCC ratifies. The ascitic neutrophil threshold for SBP (250 cells/mm3) is the widely used diagnostic cut-off and must be confirmed against the ratified national text.

rules.name: Lumbar puncture — contraindication present, do not proceed until cleared
rules.message: Do not perform lumbar puncture — a contraindication is present (raised intracranial pressure signs or coagulopathy). Correct or image first.
rules.explanation: An LP in the presence of raised intracranial pressure can precipitate cerebral herniation, and an LP in a coagulopathic or anticoagulated patient risks a spinal haematoma. Both are avoidable by acting on them before the needle, not after — imaging where raised ICP is suspected, and correcting coagulation before proceeding.
rules.requiredAction: Do not proceed. Where raised intracranial pressure is suspected, obtain neuroimaging (CT head) before LP; where a bleeding risk is present, correct coagulopathy or withhold anticoagulation and reassess. Re-evaluate the indication once the contraindication is cleared.
sourceRefs: EDLIZ — lumbar puncture: exclude raised intracranial pressure and correct bleeding risk before the procedure
Standard procedural safety practice for lumbar puncture

adaptation.whoStatement: No WHO DAK covers adult bedside procedural appropriateness; there is no source statement to adopt.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Lumbar puncture must not be performed while signs of raised intracranial pressure or a coagulopathy are present; image and/or correct first.
adaptation.rationale: The contraindication and its ordering are the safety property of the procedure — an LP into raised ICP can cone the brainstem and an LP into a bleeding diathesis causes spinal haematoma. Encoding it as an interruptive gate keeps the pre-procedure check from being skipped on a busy ward.
evidenceRefs: Standard neurology procedural practice — LP contraindications

testCases.name: raised ICP fact absent — cannot assert a contraindication
LP not being considered — rule does not apply

rules.name: Lumbar puncture — suspected CNS infection and no contraindication, LP indicated
rules.message: Lumbar puncture is indicated — suspected CNS infection with no contraindication present.
rules.explanation: In suspected meningitis or encephalitis, cerebrospinal fluid analysis is the diagnostic test that changes management. When neither raised intracranial pressure nor a bleeding risk is present, the LP should proceed promptly, because a delay to diagnosis delays targeted therapy.
rules.requiredAction: Proceed with diagnostic lumbar puncture and send CSF for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture and the indicated molecular/antigen tests. Do not delay empirical antimicrobials for the procedure where meningitis is likely.
sourceRefs: EDLIZ — meningitis: CSF examination to confirm the diagnosis
Standard procedural practice — diagnostic LP for suspected CNS infection

adaptation.nationalStatement: Where CNS infection is suspected and no contraindication is present, diagnostic lumbar puncture is indicated and should not be delayed.
adaptation.rationale: The indication is expressed as the contraindication-cleared complement of the LP safety gate, so the pack states both when to hold and when to proceed rather than only the prohibition.

rules.name: Diagnostic paracentesis — new or worsening ascites, tap to exclude SBP
rules.message: Diagnostic paracentesis is indicated — new or worsening ascites should be tapped to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
rules.explanation: Any patient presenting with new-onset ascites, or with a clinical deterioration on a background of known ascites, should have a diagnostic tap. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is common, frequently silent, and a treatable cause of decompensation — it is diagnosed on ascitic fluid, not on clinical signs.
rules.requiredAction: Perform a diagnostic ascitic tap and send fluid for cell count and differential, culture, albumin and protein. Do not defer the tap for an asymptomatic-appearing patient — SBP is frequently occult.
sourceRefs: EDLIZ — ascites and its complications: diagnostic tap for new or worsening ascites
Standard hepatology practice — diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP

adaptation.whoStatement: No WHO DAK covers adult bedside procedural appropriateness; there is no source statement to adopt.
adaptation.nationalStatement: New or worsening ascites is an indication for a diagnostic tap to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
adaptation.rationale: The rule captures the low threshold to tap that EDLIZ and hepatology practice require, because SBP is common and occult and the diagnosis is made only on fluid analysis.

rules.name: Pleural aspiration — symptomatic effusion, aspirate
rules.message: Pleural aspiration is indicated — a symptomatic effusion should be aspirated for diagnosis and relief.
rules.explanation: A pleural effusion causing breathlessness or other symptoms should be aspirated both to relieve the patient and to characterise the fluid, which is what separates a transudate from an exudate and directs the rest of the work-up. An asymptomatic small effusion may be observed, so symptoms are what tip the balance to a procedure.
rules.requiredAction: Perform pleural aspiration under the usual safeguards (image guidance where available) and send fluid for protein, LDH, cell count, Gram stain, culture and cytology as indicated. Assess symptomatic relief and re-image after the procedure.
sourceRefs: EDLIZ — pleural effusion: aspiration for diagnosis and symptom relief
Standard respiratory procedural practice — pleural aspiration

adaptation.whoStatement: No WHO DAK covers adult bedside procedural appropriateness; there is no source statement to adopt.
adaptation.nationalStatement: A symptomatic pleural effusion is an indication for aspiration for both diagnosis and symptom relief.
adaptation.rationale: Symptom presence is the discriminator between observing a small effusion and taking the diagnostic-and-therapeutic step of aspiration, so it is the fact the rule reads.

testCases.name: symptom fact absent — cannot assert an indication
pleural aspiration not being considered — rule does not apply

rules.name: Any bedside procedure — anticoagulated or coagulopathic patient needs bleeding-risk review
rules.message: Bleeding-risk review required before this bedside procedure — the patient is anticoagulated or coagulopathic.
rules.explanation: Lumbar puncture, paracentesis and pleural aspiration all breach a compartment where bleeding is hard to see and hard to control. In a patient who is anticoagulated or has a coagulopathy, the procedure needs an explicit bleeding-risk review — withhold or reverse anticoagulation, correct coagulation, or weigh the urgency against the risk — before it goes ahead.
rules.requiredAction: Hold and review the bleeding risk: check the coagulation profile and platelet count, decide on withholding or reversing anticoagulation, and document the decision to proceed, defer or correct first. This gate does not itself forbid the procedure — it requires the risk be assessed and recorded.
sourceRefs: EDLIZ — anticoagulation and procedures: assess bleeding risk before invasive procedures
Standard procedural safety practice — bleeding-risk review before bedside procedures

adaptation.whoStatement: No WHO DAK covers adult bedside procedural appropriateness; there is no source statement to adopt.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Any bedside procedure on an anticoagulated or coagulopathic patient requires a documented bleeding-risk review before it proceeds.
adaptation.rationale: This is a cross-procedure safety gate — the bleeding risk is the common hazard of every needle-based bedside procedure, so it is asserted once over all of them rather than repeated per procedure, and it requires review rather than an outright refusal because urgency can still justify proceeding after correction.
evidenceRefs: Standard procedural safety practice — periprocedural bleeding risk

rules.name: Ascitic tap interpretation — neutrophils at or above 250/mm3 means SBP
rules.message: Ascitic neutrophil count is at or above 250/mm3 — treat as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
rules.explanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed on the ascitic polymorphonuclear (neutrophil) count, not on culture, which is often negative and always slower. A count of 250 cells/mm3 or more is the threshold at which empirical treatment must start, regardless of how well the patient appears — the interpretation of the fluid is what triggers therapy.
rules.requiredAction: Start empirical antibiotics for SBP immediately (per the national regimen) and consider albumin where indicated. Do not wait for culture before treating a neutrophil count at or above the threshold.
sourceRefs: EDLIZ — spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: ascitic neutrophil count 250/mm3 threshold for treatment
Standard hepatology practice — SBP diagnosis on ascitic PMN count

rules.name: Arthrocentesis — hot joint with suspected septic arthritis
rules.message: Diagnostic arthrocentesis is indicated — hot joint with no coagulopathy; send fluid for cell count, Gram stain and culture before antibiotics when safe.
rules.explanation: Septic arthritis destroys a joint within hours to days. The definitive test is synovial fluid analysis; empirical antibiotics before the tap are reserved for patients who are critically unstable. Coagulopathy must be addressed first because haemarthrosis after a tap is difficult to evacuate.
rules.requiredAction: Aspirate the joint under aseptic technique, send cell count / differential / Gram stain / culture / crystals, then start empirical antibiotics for septic arthritis per national regimen unless an alternative diagnosis is already proven.
sourceRefs: EDLIZ — septic arthritis: aspirate before antibiotics when the patient is stable

rules.name: Bone marrow aspiration — unexplained cytopenia after peripheral work-up
rules.message: Bone marrow aspiration/trephine is indicated — unexplained cytopenia after a completed peripheral work-up.
rules.explanation: Marrow examination is the next step when cytopenia is unexplained by drugs, deficiency, infection or peripheral destruction that the blood film and basic labs have already assessed. Doing marrow before that work-up wastes a painful procedure and can miss reversible causes.
rules.requiredAction: Refer to haematology / procedures-service for marrow aspiration and trephine with the peripheral work-up attached. Do not invent a transfusion or chemotherapy plan from this indication alone.
sourceRefs: Standard haematology practice — marrow after peripheral work-up
